  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Price point fits a 90-day goal. A is priced at about $49-199/month per B2B team, so one or two paying customers is a meaningful result. B is priced at $0.05-0.10/minute or a $3-5 cap, so a single paying customer proves little and barely covers acquisition costs.",
    "A has sourced proof that budget exists in the category. Files.com bundles 'Expectations' at $199-499/mo and Nodinite cites $3,600/yr. B's comparable pricing shows the opposite: at least four sourced competitors already sit at commodity per-minute rates.",
    "B's own brief says the market is trending toward zero. It cites MacWhisper's one-time purchase, free on-device transcription and free bundling in journaling apps. B's seed thread also shows the complaining user adopted MacWhisper, a one-time purchase, rather than a pay-per-minute service.",
    "B's paid channel is mismatched with its price: Apple Search Ads CPI of $1-15+ against revenue in cents per minute. A's Google Ads benchmarks ($3-8 CPC, 3-5% click-to-demo) are also unproven for this niche, but they are more plausible against a $49-199/mo subscription.",
    "A's risks are real and documented. Files.com bundles the feature, and Definite admits teams can build it themselves 'with a cron job and a Slack webhook in an afternoon.' But they leave a narrower addressable segment rather than an outright price collapse."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's demand quotes do not show demand for the proposed product. One complains that Notion AI is too expensive and the other that Ultimate Brain is too expensive. Neither shows voice-journalers willing to pay per minute for timestamped transcription. The seed thread undercuts paid demand, since the poster settled on a one-time-purchase local tool. B's high-margin claim is marked '(presumably)' and has no source.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. A wins mainly because B's brief argues against itself, not because A's demand evidence is strong. A's demand quotes are old (2012, 2016) and about adjacent pain such as login failures and transfers going unnoticed. There is no sourced evidence that anyone would pay for a standalone sidecar, and A's own open questions concede the segment size is unknown. A's weakest point is the lack of direct evidence of willingness to pay standalone when Files.com bundles the feature and teams can self-build it for free."
